sn19.14:1.1: _Maṅguli_ is unclear. It is perhaps related to _maṅgura_ as a skin color, neither black nor brown, where the corresponding Sanskrit term is _madgura_, also spelled _maṅgura_. This is probably the common catfish *clarias magur*, which has a dingy greenish or muddy color for camouflage on the riverbed. It is a pun: what she sees are _maṅgala_ (“auspicies”), hence she is reborn like a _maṅguli_ (“catfish”).
sn19.14:1.4: _Ikkhaṇikā_ (Sanskrit _īkṣaṇikā_) is literally a “seeress”, but her putative powers extend beyond mere visions of the future. Such sorceresses were considered a “thorn” to society alongside dissemblers, cheats, gamblers, and palmists (Manu 9.258). Medhātithi comments that they would con wealthy men out of money by promising them the favors of the gods, or casting spells. Jain texts say sorceresses worked by jingling a small bell under their ear, at the sound of which their tutelary spirit would approach and whisper secrets. The Pali commentary likewise says she does the bidding of her _yakkha_ familiar: “It seems they do a slave-yakkha’s work, saying, ‘When such and such a bali ritual is performed, you will certainly prosper.’ Having taken people’s scents and flowers, etc. by fraud, she made them accept bad view, wrong view. Therefore as her share of kamma, she became foul-smelling from stealing scents and flowers, and became ugly, deformed, and hideous from making them accept a wrong view.” Thus the word comes full circle to approximate the modern sense of “catfishing”. Nonetheless, Kautilya, ever the pragmatist, is not above enlisting them in the services of the state for the dissemination of fake news (Arthaśāstra 13.1.7). The background story to [ja126]() tells how such a sorceress was enlisted by a princess to deploy faked magical powers to ensure she would end up with her lover. Her claimed powers in this story include divination of possession, exorcism, and revivifying a corpse with a malevolent spirit.
